paragraphs: Although the desire to acquire the good things of this world is the dominant passion of the American people, there are certain sudden outbreaks when their souls seem to burst the bonds of matter that hold them and soar impetuously toward heaven. In all the States of the Union, but especially in the half-settled country of the Far West, you meet wandering preachers who peddle the word of God from place to place. Whole families, old men, women and children alike, cross rough passes and untrodden wilds, coming from a great distance to join a camp meeting. There, for several days and nights, they forget entirely the cares of business and even the most pressing needs of the body as they listen to these sermons. Here and there in American society you meet men full of a fanatical and almost wild enthusiasm that hardly exists in Europe. From time to time strange sects arise that try to cut out extraordinary paths to eternal happiness. Religious insanity is very common in the United States.

These facts should not surprise us. It was not man who put into himself the taste for the infinite and the love of the immortal. Those lofty instincts are not the product of his whim. Their firm foundation lies in human nature, and they exist in spite of his efforts. He may thwart and distort them, but he cannot destroy them. The soul has needs that must be satisfied. However much trouble is taken to distract it from itself, it soon grows weary, restless and uneasy amid the pleasures of the senses. If the faculties of the great majority of mankind were ever bent exclusively on material objects, we could expect a tremendous reaction in the souls of some men. They would drift far and wide in the world of spirits, for fear of staying shackled by the tight bondage of the body.

It is not surprising, then, that in a community whose thoughts tend toward the earth, a small number of people should turn their eyes to heaven. I would be surprised if mysticism did not soon make some progress among a people wholly occupied with promoting its own worldly welfare. It is said that the deserts of the Thebaid were peopled by the persecutions of the emperors and the massacres of the Circus. I would rather say that they were peopled by the luxuries of Rome and the Epicurean philosophy of Greece. Suppose the social condition, the present circumstances and the laws of the Americans did not confine their minds so tightly to the pursuit of worldly welfare. Then they would probably show more restraint and more experience whenever their attention turns to immaterial things, and they would check themselves without difficulty. But they feel imprisoned within limits that, it seems, they will never be allowed to cross. As soon as they do cross them, their minds do not know where to settle, and they often rush unrestrained beyond the bounds of common sense.
